source: Amodio, Brea, Farrar, Ostojic, Clayton (2021) Testing two competing hypotheses for Eurasian jays' caching for the future
finding: Background part: the scrub-jay planning results have three rival readings. Future Planning (recall what-where-when and cache for the future), Mnemonic Association (long-delay learning from earlier recoveries), and Compensatory Caching (spread each food away from places it was seen). Mnemonic Association cannot explain Raby 2007 because the jays cached only once. Compensatory Caching can.
numbers: No new data in this line. Raby 2007 as described here: Exp 1, six days in compartment A or C with food in the first two hours only in one; Exp 2, each compartment tied to one food. One test caching session each.
limits: Secondary description of Raby 2007 (the paper itself was not opened). Compensatory Caching came from a personal communication cited in a review.
agent_relevance: Any claim of planning needs a control for a cheap fixed rule. A plan-like output can come from a spread-out default.

source: Amodio, Brea, Farrar, Ostojic, Clayton (2021) Testing two competing hypotheses for Eurasian jays' caching for the future
finding: Experiment 1: Eurasian jays in a design where Future Planning and Compensatory Caching predict opposite caching across three compartments (two foods rotating on a 2-day cycle, compartments on a 3-day cycle, 9 experience days, one test). Neither hypothesis fit. Caching depended on bird and food, not on compartment.
numbers: 6 birds reached the test (9 started). Posterior of best model (bird x food, no compartment effect) = 0.997. Best Future Planning model = 0.0014. Compensatory Caching = 0.00001. Only one bird (Lisbon) cached as Future Planning predicts.
limits: Small N. Design was more complex than Raby 2007, so it is not a direct replication.
agent_relevance: Bayesian model comparison against a null rule can show that an apparent planning effect is absent. Use it when we test planning in the agent.

source: Amodio, Brea, Farrar, Ostojic, Clayton (2021) Testing two competing hypotheses for Eurasian jays' caching for the future
finding: Experiment 2 (preregistered, lower load: food vs no food in each compartment). Again the best model was uniform caching over compartments. Compensatory Caching beat Future Planning, but neither beat uniform.
numbers: 7 birds tested. Posterior: compartment-independent 0.72, Compensatory Caching 0.16, Future Planning 0.002. Wellington, Rome and partly Lisbon fit Compensatory Caching. Caracas, Washington, Quito spread caches almost equally.
limits: Preregistered at OSF before the test. N still 7. Individual differences are large.
agent_relevance: Report per-individual patterns, not only group means. Single runs of an agent can hide a mix of strategies.

source: Amodio, Brea, Farrar, Ostojic, Clayton (2021) Testing two competing hypotheses for Eurasian jays' caching for the future
finding: Authors say the clash with Raby 2007 cannot be explained yet and ask for direct replication of both. Candidate causes: group housing (jays could see others using the rooms), a food-place link that changed every few days (low ecological fit), and higher cognitive load.
numbers: Raby 2007 scrub-jays were housed in pairs in 2 x 1 x 1 m cages. These jays lived as a group in a 20 x 10 x 3 m aviary. Exp 1 required tracking food over three locations on short cycles.
limits: The authors note neither hypothesis states a load limit, so the load excuse is not testable as framed.
agent_relevance: Boundary conditions matter: the same ability claim can fail under a harder or more dynamic version of the task. Test the agent at several loads.

source: Thom and Clayton (2014) No evidence of temporal preferences in caching by Western scrub-jays (Aphelocoma californica)
finding: Scrub-jays that plan for future desires showed no preference to cache where recovery would come sooner. Two experiments with delays from 7 minutes to 49 hours.
numbers: Exp 2: mean caches (of 20 worms) in the last three trials 5.24 (7 min), 4.97 (26 h), 5.45 (7-SR condition). F(1.37, 15.07) = 0.123, p = .808. No bird cached all 20. Exp 1: 1 h, 25 h and 49 h trays got similar caching. Group size not stated in the passages read, only implied by the df.
limits: Null result. Authors admit a failure to learn is not an inability to learn. Caching persists even without reinforcement.
agent_relevance: Planning in jays may reach only the near future (they cite 210 min from Correia 2007). Do not assume planning scales with horizon.

source: Thom and Clayton (2014) No evidence of temporal preferences in caching by Western scrub-jays (Aphelocoma californica)
finding: Three readings of the null: delays too short to matter, birds oblivious to delay length, or birds learned the delay and were indifferent. Authors lean to: birds tell present from future but not how far into the future.
numbers: Correia 2007 birds anticipated the recovery context 210 min ahead. Prospective caching has been shown after as few as 1 to 3 prior encounters with a tray.
limits: Speculative account that the authors themselves call speculative.
agent_relevance: Test our agent for horizon sensitivity (does it weigh a payoff 3 steps away differently from 30?). Planning without a sense of distance is a known animal result.

source: Martin, Martin, Roberts, Sherry (2021) No evidence for future planning in Canada jays (Perisoreus canadensis)
finding: Canada jays tested with the Raby-style procedure did not cache where food would be missing. They cached where food was usually available, the opposite of the scrub-jay pattern.
numbers: Counts and N not read: only the abstract was obtained (full text server errored).
limits: Abstract only. Species and housing differ from Raby 2007, so this is a mixed result across species.
agent_relevance: The scrub-jay result is not general across caching corvids. Treat a single-species effect as weak evidence for a general ability.

source: Cheke and Clayton (2012) Eurasian jays (Garrulus glandarius) overcome their current desires to anticipate two distinct future needs and plan for them appropriately
finding: Eurasian jays distinguished two distinct future desires and cached for each despite a conflicting current motivation. Authors say this answers criticisms of earlier work and suggest associative learning and future-oriented cognition may combine.
numbers: Numbers not read: only the abstract was obtained (full text server errored).
limits: Abstract only. Amodio 2021 later lists long-delay learning as a standing alternative for this design.
agent_relevance: Learning and planning may not be exclusive: a scaffold can use both a learned rule and an explicit forecast.

source: Boeckle, Schiestl, Frohnwieser, Gruber, Miller, Suddendorf, Gray, Taylor, Clayton (2020) New Caledonian crows plan for specific future tool use
finding: A test built to separate planning from present preference. The same tools were the right choice in one condition and a distractor in the next. Three of four trained crows chose the right tool for the future problem.
numbers: Four of six crows tested (nine started) reached criterion in 20 to 25 trials. In the critical test 9/10, 7/10 and 7/10 correct (five options, chance 20%, p < 0.001) for three crows. One crow scored 3/10 (p = 0.429).
limits: Only 4 of 9 birds passed training. All successful birds were female. Authors concede associative learning cannot be fully excluded. Distractor food may have been learned away. Reanalysis as 3 options (chance 33%) kept the result.
agent_relevance: Design to adopt: reuse the same item as solution and distractor across trials so value-based rules fail. Use this in agent tests of planning.

source: Boeckle et al. (2020) New Caledonian crows plan for specific future tool use (background paragraph on children)
finding: Concern about earlier spoon-test studies: the chosen tool may have higher present value, not a future image. A child study found under-fives chose at chance between two high-value objects when only one solved the observed problem.
numbers: Children under five at chance (value not given in the passage read).
limits: Secondary report of the child study. The child paper was not opened here.
agent_relevance: A single-choice tool test can give false positives. Our planning probes should keep option value equal.

source: Redshaw and Suddendorf (2013) Foresight beyond the very next event: four-year-olds can link past and deferred future episodes
finding: Four-year-olds saw a problem in one room, were distracted for 15 min, then chose an item for a bucket to be taken back after a 5-minute timer. Success fell when the future problem was deferred but stayed above chance.
numbers: Instant condition 91.7% correct, delayed 50%, chance 16.7% (chi2(1) = 97.20 and 19.20, both p < 0.001). Condition effect F(1,22) = 12.79, p = 0.002 (about 24 children). 25% of children referred to future use; all of them chose correctly.
limits: Children who did not mention the future: one third chose correctly, not above chance (p = 0.058). Small sample, two tasks.
agent_relevance: The human baseline is partial: even 4-year-olds are at about 50% on a deferred version. Do not set a human-perfect bar.

source: Redshaw and Suddendorf (2013) Foresight beyond the very next event
finding: Authors argue one mechanism may serve the next event and a deferred one: delayed 50% (chance 16.7%) matches 58.3% (chance 33.3%) in an earlier study where the future episode came right after the act.
numbers: 50% vs 58.3% success.
limits: Cross-study comparison with different chance levels. Not a test.
agent_relevance: Planning may mainly need the right past episode pulled into working memory. Retrieval quality is a lever for an agent.

source: Redshaw, Taylor, Suddendorf (2017) Flexible planning in ravens?
finding: Commentary on Kabadayi and Osvath 2017: asks whether leaner alternatives explain the ravens' choice of items for future rewards.
numbers: No numbers read (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only. Author list taken from memory, check before citing.
agent_relevance: Pairs with Boeckle 2020: the critique led to a tighter test design.

source: Suddendorf and Corballis (2010) Behavioural evidence for mental time travel in nonhuman animals (Behav Brain Res)
finding: Review of animal foresight data. Concluded that evidence for episodic-type foresight was equivocal and proposed specific experimental criteria.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Abstract only. Author names added from memory, check before citing.
agent_relevance: A criteria list (flexible, novel, not driven by current need) can serve as an acceptance test for agent planning claims.

source: Eurasian jays show episodic-like memory through the incidental encoding of information (PLOS ONE 2024)
finding: Eurasian jays used unexpected, incidentally encoded visual information about an experimenter's baiting to choose a cup. Control test: they used spatial information but not visual information.
numbers: 7 jays. Main test above chance (binomial GLMM p < 0.001). No effect of condition (F(2,14) = 0.334, p = 0.721) or trial (F(1,14) = 0.476, p = 0.501). Control: spatial above chance (p < 0.001), visual p = 0.151.
limits: Birds were trained on the baiting-then-choice routine, so the test may no longer be truly unexpected. Backward-looking memory, not planning.
agent_relevance: Evidence for the memory half of mental time travel. Memory of incidental detail is a separate ability from planning.

source: Is episodic-like memory like episodic memory? (Phil Trans R Soc B 2024 review)
finding: Review concludes the evidence is mixed and recommends combining several paradigms. On future-oriented tasks it says rats and rhesus macaques appear to fail a choose-for-future-desire task, squirrel monkeys succeeded, and some paradigms were criticised or failed to replicate. It notes the Clayton and Suddendorf pre-registered spoon test with New Caledonian crows.
numbers: No pooled effect sizes. Cites Amodio 2021 and Martin 2021 (Canada jays) as non-supporting data.
limits: Read selected sections only, not every section.
agent_relevance: Expert consensus is mixed, not settled. Use hedged wording in our notes.

source: Social influences on delayed gratification in New Caledonian crows and Eurasian jays (PLOS ONE 2023)
finding: A rival present changes the choice. Crows waited for the better delayed reward in all conditions. Jays waited when alone but took the poor immediate reward when a competitor or non-competitor was present.
numbers: 6 crows, 5 jays. Species x condition chi2(2) = 60.36, p < 0.0001. Jays alone vs with competitor z = 7.27, p < 0.0001. All 6 crows chose delayed in all 3 conditions. No jay chose delayed significantly when anyone was present.
limits: Crows and jays differed in origin, housing and training, which the authors list as confounds.
agent_relevance: Future-directed choice is sensitive to social pressure. Test a scaffold's patience under pressure, not only alone.

source: Siberian flying squirrels do not anticipate future resource abundance (BMC Ecology 2016)
finding: A field test of anticipation in a mammal. Summer litters followed past food (alder catkins), not future food. Future alder pollen had a negative effect.
numbers: 733 litters; about 15% of mothers produced summer litters (93 of 640 females). Past alder coefficient 1.5 (95% CI 1.1 to 2.1). Future alder -0.30 (CI -0.05 to -0.65). Adding future variables worsened fit (delta AIC 26 for alder, 29 for birch).
limits: Observational. Reproduction, not cognition. Some summer litters probably missed.
agent_relevance: Forward-looking behaviour can be a response to present condition. Check present-state explanations first.

source: Meta-analysis: Promoting farsighted decisions via episodic future thinking (J Exp Psychol Gen 2022)
finding: Imagining future events makes people choose long-term gains more. Medium effect, not explained by demand effects or by other future thinking.
numbers: 174 effect sizes from 48 articles. g = 0.44, 95% CI [0.33, 0.55] after adjusting for publication bias. Stronger for positive, vivid, choice-related imagery. Larger in impulsive samples such as obesity.
limits: Abstract only. Mostly self-report choices.
agent_relevance: Concrete, positive, task-linked simulation changes choice. A scaffold step that asks for a vivid, specific future scene is the human analogue.

source: Meta-analysis: effects of episodic future thinking on delay discounting (Q J Exp Psychol 2022)
finding: Episodic future thinking lowers delay discounting. The effect depends on valence: positive imagery works, neutral or negative does not.
numbers: 47 studies, 63 contrasts. Hedges g = 0.52 overall. Positive EFT g = 0.64, valence not stated g = 0.28, neutral or negative g = -0.03. Control task and discounting-task features also moderated.
limits: Abstract only. The paper says earlier results were inconsistent.
agent_relevance: Direction of the simulated future matters. Prompting for a neutral or negative future may give no benefit.

source: Poonsiriwong et al. (2025) Simulating Life Paths with Digital Twins: AI-Generated Future Selves Influence Decision-Making and Expand Human Choice
finding: LLM-driven future-self avatars (age-progressed face, cloned voice, LLM dialogue) shifted young adults' pending decisions. A system-generated third option was adopted far more than in control.
numbers: N = 192 aged 18 to 28, five arms (control 37, A 38, B 39, A+B 38, A+B+C 40). Two-sided avatar switch rate 34.2% vs 10.8% control (p = 0.015). Novel Option C chosen 20.0% vs 2.7% (p = 0.019). Single-sided effects only marginal (p < 0.1).
limits: Short-term stated intention, no follow-up of real outcomes. Many tests, several marginal at p < 0.1. Authors raise persuasion concerns.
agent_relevance: Showing a simulated future to a person can change choices. Our agent should not push a simulated future without showing its uncertainty.

source: Poonsiriwong et al. (2025) Simulating Life Paths with Digital Twins
finding: Which part of vividness works: evaluative reasoning and meaning outranked affect and visual realism. Decisional conflict and agency changed after the avatars.
numbers: Friedman chi2 = 91.24, p < 0.001, Kendall's W = 0.158. Evaluative vs affective d = -0.568, evaluative vs visual d = -0.438 (both p < 0.001). Decision-change model pseudo R2 = 0.25.
limits: Self-report ratings. Effect sizes as printed in the paper.
agent_relevance: The content of a simulation (consequences, values) matters more than rendering polish.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) TriggerBench: Investigating Prospective Memory for Large Language Models
finding: On matched contexts, retrospective memory is near perfect while prospective memory (acting on a latent constraint without a prompt) drops as context grows.
numbers: Retrospective memory about 98% or more up to 100K tokens. Prospective accuracy falls sharply as context grows from 20K to 100K tokens (curve in the paper's figure).
limits: Synthetic scenarios scored by an LLM judge. Exact per-model numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Remembering to act later is a distinct failure from forgetting. Add an explicit step that re-checks stored commitments.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) TriggerBench
finding: A competing user request wipes out prospective recall (dual-task interference). Prospective accuracy also tracked spare reasoning budget.
numbers: Drops of up to 73 points (GPT-4o) and 71 points (Qwen3-32B) on the Attention Recovery dimension. At 30 to 50K tokens, PM accuracy 47.1% when the paired AIME-2025 answer was correct (n = 272) vs 37.8% when wrong (n = 143), a 9.3 point gap.
limits: Correlational link with the math answer.
agent_relevance: Do the foreground task and the deferred-commitment check as separate steps. A busy agent drops its latent constraints.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) TriggerBench
finding: Stronger reasoning raises proactive recall but models can drift into an always-remind rule, raising false alarms. Precision and recall trade off.
numbers: Per-model figures are in the paper's appendix tables; not extracted here.
limits: Prompt aggressiveness moves the operating point more than it improves overall skill, per the authors' ablation.
agent_relevance: Measure false alarms as well as hits when scoring any remember-to-act feature.

source: Liu and Gabriel (2026) PM-Bench: Evaluating Prospective Memory in LLM Agents
finding: A seven-day simulated week (Virtual Week style) tests deferred intentions, updates and hidden-state monitoring. Best of eight models and eight configurations reached only 65.1% Set-F1. No single strategy dominated across models.
numbers: Best: GPT-5.4 single agent with optional heartbeat, macro Set-F1 65.1%, cross-day hit 50.0%, update 44.4%. Todo-ledger variant 62.8% with fewest false positives. Best hidden-channel monitoring hit rate 15.8% in one setup.
limits: Synthetic benchmark. Scores as printed in the paper.
agent_relevance: An external to-do ledger is the cheapest effective support, matching the schema idea of explicit state.

source: Zhao and Wu (2026) Making Prospective Memory SLM-Shaped: Typed Intention Stores for Small-Model Agents
finding: A typed store of deferred intentions with code-run lifecycle (Form, Revise, Filter, Decide) lifted PM-Bench scores. Standard retrospective memory tools did not.
numbers: DeepSeek-Chat Set-F1: no store 67.7, naive RAG 46.5, Mem0 48.7, A-Mem 54.1, Letta 52.2, LightMem-style 51.5, MemoryOS-style 58.3, PIS 82.9 (table text garbled in extraction; abstract confirms 82.9). Gemma-E2B: 4.2 without store, at most 6.6 with retrospective memory, 66.2 with PIS.
limits: Preprint, one benchmark, upstream memory systems re-implemented as pattern adapters, not the full servers.
agent_relevance: Memory that stores the past can hurt a prospective task. Our schema should hold commitments as typed objects, not free notes.

source: Pasternak et al. (2025, v4 2026) Beyond Reactivity: Measuring Proactive Problem Solving in LLM Agents (PROBE)
finding: Anticipating a user need over a long horizon (search, find bottleneck, act) is hard for frontier models. The weakest step is root cause identification.
numbers: Best end-to-end 40%, reached by both GPT-5 and Claude Opus 4.1. Incorrect root cause averages 73.8% of identification failures. Annotator agreement 85% and 81% (Fleiss kappa 0.7 and 0.62).
limits: Preprint benchmark with its own pipeline.
agent_relevance: Foresight of needs fails mostly at diagnosis, not at carrying out the fix.

source: Pink et al. (2025) Position: Episodic Memory is the Missing Piece for Long-Term LLM Agents
finding: Position paper: argues LLM agents need episodic memory with five properties and a roadmap. It reports no new measurements.
numbers: No experiments. Names single-shot learning, long-term storage and explicit reasoning among the properties.
limits: Position paper. The text read does not treat future simulation or planning directly.
agent_relevance: Gives a vocabulary for the memory half of mental time travel but no evidence on the future half.
